content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies "representation bias" in the context of long-tailed recognition (LTR) and argues that "representation bias" has not yet been researched. Moreover, the paper reports that intra-class variance in representation space is negatively correlated to class frequency, and reveals that high tail variance is due to spurious correlations learned by deep models. To counter representation bias, it proposes the Learned Nearest-Class-Mean (NCM) which jointly learns class centroids minimizing average class-distance normalized variance. Lastly, the paper uses logit adjustment technique in the NCM classifier to achieve higher tail class margin. Experiments show the proposed method achieves 6% gain over state-of-the-art in two LTR benchmarks, CIFAR100-LT and ImageNet-LT.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength 
- The paper studies an important problem (Long-Tailed Recognition, LTR) as data in the real world oftentimes follows a long-tailed distribution.
- The paper explores new methods based on learning Nearest Class Mean, and adopts other techniques atop of it such as logit adjustment. It items like a good try by combining these techniques in the context of LTR.

Weaknesses
- Clarity and quality of the paper should be improved. See detailed in the next box.
- The paper misses important citations of the LTR literature. See detailed in the next box.
- The paper lacks novelty. For example, it combines learning NCM and logit adjustment, both are known and the latter has been applied to LTR.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
"Representation bias" is not clearly defined, although the Abstract states that "representation bias has not yet been researched". How to justify the representation is biased, and how to measure the degree of representation bias?

The paper states that "intra-class variance in representation space is negatively correlated to class frequency". To compute intra-class variance, did the authors use training examples or testing examples? In Figure 1, are the points representing training data or testing data?

It is not clear what "spurious correlations" mean in the Abstract. How to justify that "high-tail variance is due to spurious correlations"? Can authors give some visual examples to illustrate this issue?

The format of citations is quite confusing. Below are a few examples in the first paragraph -- 

- Past decades have seen a lot of research in class-imbalanced learning He & Garcia (2009), a challenge that is shared by a diverse set of problems ranging from image classification Van Horn & Perona (2017); Wang et al. (2017), face recognition Yin et al. (2019) and object detection Lin et al. (2017) to sentiment analysisMaas et al. (2011) and anomaly detectionChandola et al. (2009). 
- They seek to rectify head class bias in the classifier through data-resampling Kang et al. (2020), loss reshaping Ren et al. (2020); Menon et al. (2021); Samuel & Chechik (2021), ensemble-based models Xiang et al. (2020); Wang et al. (2020); Zhou et al. (2020), and knowledge transfer Liu et al. (2019; 2021).

As the paper explores long-tailed recognition (LTR), it misses citations. For example [R1] explores weight regularization for LTR by using weight decay and Max-Norm regularizes, and concludes that LTR literature had not sufficiently tune weight decay which turned out to be crucial for LTR. Importantly, [R1] is simpler and achieves better results on the benchmarking datasets than the method proposed in this paper. Authors should discuss and compare [R1], otherwise it is not clear whether the performance gain by the proposed method is owing to better regularization or the designed NCM and logit adjustment techniques.
[R1] Alshammari, et al., "Long-Tailed Recognition via Weight Balancing", CVPR 2022

Figure 3 is hard to follow. What do the values mean in the heatmap? Aren't negative values significant as they have large absolute values?

Eq. (4): What is the principle behind using sigmoid function to transform class-specific projection parameters? 

Section 4: What is regular sampling and uniform sampling? Does uniform sampling mean "class-balanced sampling" as this is a common practice in the two-stage LTR methods?

On ImageNet-LT, why use ResNet-10 backbone as this is a rather small network? Other LTR methods use ResNet50.

Table 1: Is "Softmax" using two-stage training? [R1] tuned weight decay in the two-stage training and used softmax classifier, and achieves better performance than what reported here. Can authors have a look and provide any comments?
content.summary_of_the_review: Based on the above detailed comments, I'd reject this paper, which (1) misses important citations, (2) has confusing statements and claims, and (3) lacks novelty/contributions to the field of long-tailed recognition.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
(1) This paper aims to address the long-tailed recognition problem. 
      Based on the observation that intra-class variance in representation space is negatively correlated to class frequency, the Learned Nearest-Class-Mean (NCM) is proposed.    

(2) Experiments are conducted on CIFAR-LT and ImageNet-LT. Some improvements are obtained compared with some previous methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:  
(1) The analysis of representation bias is interesting.     
(2) The method is simple to implement.    
(3) The paper writes clear and is easy to follow.   


Weakness:      
(1) The paper claims that it achieves state-of-the-art. However, some previous state-of-the-art methods are not compared, like PaCo [1], and RIDE [2], ACE [3]. The baselines are too weak to compare.       

[1] Parametric Contrastive Learning. ICCV 2021.    
[2] Long-tailed Recognition by Routing Diverse Distribution-Aware Experts. ICLR 2021.     
[3] ACE: Ally Complementary Experts for Solving Long-Tailed Recognition in One-Shot. ICCV 2021.     

(2) The paper aims to relieve the representation bias. However, from their algorithm, it trains the model with cross-entropy and uniform sampling and then fixes the representation and uses the proposed Learned Nearest-Class-Mean to learn the classifier. From my understanding, once the representation is fixed, how can we relieve the representation bias?    

Maybe pertaining or end-to-end learning methods can solve the representation bias issue.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper aims to improve model performance on long-tailed data by relieving the representation bias issue.
However, some important comparisons with previous work are missed. 
Moreover, whether the proposed Learned Nearest-Class-Mean solves the representation bias problem is not clear.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper deals with the problem of imbalanced intra-class variance in long-tailed recognition, named “representation bias” and proposes learned Nearest-Class-Mean (NCM) to solve it. Specifically, this method learns centroids by minimizing average class-distance normalized variance. Learned NCM can be combined with label-aware margin technique and extended to multiple centroids per class as well.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. The paper is well-written and easy to follow.

2. The paper conducts an empirical study to clearly explain the representation bias problem.

Weaknesses:
1. The motivation of the paper is unclear.
This paper claims that the high tail variance is caused by noise or spurious correlations, leading to representation bias and causes low performance of the model. This point needs more clarification. Moreover, this paper claims that the learned NCM classifier with class-balanced sampling and frozen representation avoids the issue of imbalanced classifier norm. It is confusing as the imbalanced classifier norm has been addressed by training a softmax classifier with class-balanced sampling, such as in [1]. And, it is not clear at all whether the representation quality is improved or not with the learned NCM classifier.

2. The novelty of proposed method is very limited. 
The proposed modules have been employed by some existing works in long-tailed recognition. The proposed learned NCM could be seen as CRT [1] with replacing the classifier by NCM and the paper does not analyze how NCM over-performs softmax classifier to make the replacement meaningful. Moreover, learned NCM with class-ware margin can be considered as a variant of LDAM [2] or Balanced Softmax [3]. It is not a significant contribution as margin-based loss has been widely employed in long-tailed recognition [2,3,4] while NCM with margin has been discussed by [5]. The multiple centroids extension of learned NCM is fairly straightforward ($u_j^i=u_j+\delta_i$ in which $u_j^i$ is the centroid) and very similar to the incremental variant of  as which is an incremental edition of multiple softmax of [6] ($w_j^i=w_j+\delta_i$ in which $w_j^i$ is the weight of classifier).
Another concern is, as logit adjustment only adjusts $P(y|x)$, why not try to improve logit adjustment [5] with learned NCM?

3. The empirical improvement is marginal and instable.
The learned NCM only has marginal performance improvement in the experiments, i.e. less than 0.2% of all settings expect on CIFAR-100-LT (IR:200) compared with CRT (noted as Decoupling in this paper). And, the experimental performance is not very stable, i.e. under the most usual setting (IR:100), the “Learned-NCM + Logit Adjustment” on CIFAR-100-LT and “Learned-NCM” on CIFAR-10-LT are not better than CRT, and it is even marginally worse than CRT on ImageNet-LT. Considering the baseline NCM is generally stronger than softmax classifier in the experiments, i.e. 46.0 vs 48.7 on CIFAR-100-LT (IR:100) and 41.2 vs 43.4 on CIFAR-100-LT (IR:200), and comparing with the results from [5], the empirical results in this paper can hardly convince the community.

4. Improper claims and confusing names. 
There are some improper claims, e.g., “representation bias has not yet been researched”，“this intriguing observation has not been explored in prior work”, etc. As far as I know, similar issues have already been discussed by lots of previous works, such as [5], [7].
There are also some confusing names, e.g., “Decouping” may cause misunderstanding as the original paper [1] proposes four decoupling methods including CRT;  the name “learned NCM+logits adjustment” is somewhat confusing as the margin of learned NCM has different operations and purposes from logits adjustment [4].

5. Missing methods in comparative study.
As a two-stage method, learned NCM , which is claimed state-of-the-art, should be compared with  recent representative two-stage methods e.g. DRO-LT [5] and Disalign [6], which is easy to implement as their official codes have been released. Considering learned NCM is based on a strong baseline as the result of softmax classifier is much better than previous method (e.g. 46.0 vs 38.32 in DRO-LT [5] on CIFAR-100-LT (IR:100)), the results of the compared methods should be reproduced under the same condition instead of only comparing with the number reported in the original paper.

6. Missing experiment details.
Complete optimization details such as batchsize, weight decay etc. are missing. The paper explains it follows prior work but without citation.

7. Missing references. 
The most recent related works are not cited in this paper. In fact, there are no reference papers after 2021. This is not acceptable as a top conference submission.

[1] Decoupling representation and classifier for long-tailed recognition, ICLR 2020.

[2] Learning imbalanced datasets with label-distribution-aware margin loss, NeurIPS 2019.

[3] Balanced meta-softmax for long-tailed visual recognition, NeurIPS 2020.

[4] Long-tail learning via logit adjustment, ICLR 2021.

[5] Distributional robustness loss for long-tail learning, CVPR 2021.

[6] A Unified Framework for Long-tail Visual Recognition, CVPR21.

[7] Identifying and Compensating for Feature Deviation in Imbalanced Deep Learning, arXiv 2001.01385.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper uses a center loss like approach on feature representations to balance the learning for long-tail distributed data. One of the contribution is learnable feature centroids (so-called learned nearest class mean) approach.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: I think this paper is not ready for submission and lacks necessary details. For example, for Figure 2, how are the feature representations aquaired? Are they generated by plain models or other long-tail models? Figure 3 doesn't show anything. Notations of equations are not sufficiently annotated or described. Novelty of the proposed method is limited. I like the idea of learnable centroids, but in general, it is just a center loss variant, which is fine unless the results are good. However, according to the reported results, the improvements are very limited compared to other baselines. In addition, I don't think the discussion on representation bias, especially the dispersion of class features, is new. At least in OLTR, they have already talked about similar things and already applied a variant center loss to the model. Finally, many state-of-the-art methods like RIDE and TADE are not compared more discussed.

content.title: Learned Nearest-Class-Mean for Biased Representations in Long-Tailed Recognition
content.TL;DR: Representations in long-tailed recognition exhibit high tail variance; propose Learned NCM to mitigate representation bias.
content.abstract: The problem of long-tailed recognition (LTR) has received attention in recent years due to the fundamental power-law distribution of objects in the real-world. While classifier bias in LTR has been addressed by many works, representation bias has not yet been researched. At the same time, most recent works use softmax classifiers that are unable to cope with representation bias. In this work, we address these shortcomings by firstly making the key observation that intra-class variance in representation space is negatively correlated to class frequency, leading to biased representations; our analysis reveals that high tail variance is due to spurious correlations learned by deep models. Secondly, to counter representation bias, we propose the Learned Nearest-Class-Mean (NCM), which overcomes uncertainty in empirical centroid estimates and jointly learns centroids minimizing average class-distance normalized variance. Further, we adapt the logit adjustment technique in the NCM framework to achieve higher tail class margin. Our Learned NCM with Logit Adjustment achieves 6\% gain over state-of-the-art in tail accuracy on the benchmark CIFAR100-LT and ImageNet-LT datasets.
